title: Sometimes “I’m Just Being Honest” Means “I Never Learned to Control My Tongue.”
paragraphs:
Sometimes “I’m Just Being Honest” Means “I Never Learned to Control My Tongue.”
You can tell the truth and still sin with the way you tell it. Sometimes the sentence we call “honesty” is simply cruelty wearing a respectable Christian name.
“I’m just being honest.”
Four words.

Four words that have ended friendships, humiliated spouses, wounded children, divided churches, embarrassed people in public, and left wounds that lasted far longer than the conversation that caused them.
Maybe you have heard them.
Maybe you have said them.
Maybe someone looked directly at the part of you that was already bleeding, pressed their finger into it, and then defended themselves with those four words:
“I’m just being honest.”
And perhaps the most uncomfortable possibility is this...
Sometimes we really were telling the truth.
But we were not speaking like Jesus.
That distinction matters more than many Christians realize.
Because Scripture never gives us permission to baptize cruelty simply because the information coming out of our mouth happens to be factually correct.
A statement can be technically true and spiritually reckless.
You can have the right facts and the wrong heart.
You can expose something real and still expose it for the wrong reason.
You can win the argument and wound the person.
You can say, “But I didn’t lie,” while completely missing the question God may actually be asking:
Why did you need to say it like that?
Proverbs gives us an image so violent that we should never again think careless speech is a small spiritual issue.
The Hebrew of Proverbs 12:18 reads:
יֵשׁ בּוֹטֶה כְּמַדְקְרוֹת חָרֶב וּלְשׁוֹן חֲכָמִים מַרְפֵּא
Yesh boteh kemadqerot charev, uleshon chachamim marpe.
The King James Version renders it:
“There is that speaketh like the piercings of a sword: but the tongue of the wise is health.”
Modern translations commonly capture the first image as reckless or rash speech being like the thrusts of a sword.
Do not rush past that picture.
A sword.
God could have compared careless words to rain.
He could have compared them to dust.
He could have described them merely as annoying or unpleasant.
Instead, wisdom gives us the picture of something penetrating flesh.
The Hebrew expression behind the reckless speaker carries the idea of blurting or speaking rashly. The image that follows is madqerot cherev—the piercings or thrusts of a sword.
Then comes the breathtaking contrast:
uleshon chachamim marpe.
“But the tongue of the wise is healing.”
Marpe carries the sense of healing, health, cure, or remedy.
Two tongues.
Two possibilities.
One pierces.
One heals.
And here is what should disturb us:
Both mouths may be saying something true.
The dividing line in this proverb is not simply truth versus falsehood.
It is reckless speech versus wise speech.
That means biblical wisdom asks a question our culture often refuses to ask:
Not only, “Is it true?”
But also...
“Why am I saying it?”
“Does this need to be said?”
“Does it need to be said now?”
“Does it need to be said publicly?”
“Am I trying to restore this person—or punish them?”
“Am I speaking because I love them—or because hurting them will make me feel powerful for thirty seconds?”
That last question is painful.
Because sometimes “honesty” is revenge with clean hands.
We were angry.
We wanted them to feel what they made us feel.
We knew exactly which insecurity to touch.
Exactly which failure to mention.
Exactly which old wound to reopen.
Exactly which sentence would silence the room.
And then we said it.
The face changed.
The eyes dropped.
The room became quiet.
Something inside the other person collapsed.
And because what we said was technically accurate, we told ourselves we had done nothing wrong.
“I only told the truth.”
But truth was never given to us as a weapon for satisfying our flesh.
The New Testament refuses to separate truth from love.
Paul tells believers to be “speaking the truth in love” in Ephesians 4:15.
Notice what Christianity does not require us to choose between.
Truth or love.
Biblical love does not require lying.
Biblical truth does not require cruelty.
Jesus embodies both perfectly.
John describes Him as “full of grace and truth.”
Not fifty percent grace and fifty percent truth.
Not grace when people behaved and truth when they irritated Him.
Grace and truth dwelling perfectly together in one Person.
Jesus could confront sin with terrifying clarity.
He could expose hypocrisy.
He could call people to repentance.
He never needed to dilute holiness to appear compassionate.
Yet look at what happened when broken people encountered Him.
A woman caught in adultery was brought before Him publicly.
Her sin was real.
Jesus did not rename adultery.
He did not declare sin harmless.
But neither did He join the crowd eager to destroy her.
After her accusers disappeared, He told her that He did not condemn her and commanded her to leave her life of sin.
Grace did not erase truth.
Truth did not erase grace.
Grace rescued her from condemnation.
Truth called her into transformation.
That is Jesus.
And some of us need to admit that what we have called “boldness” looks very little like Him.
We have confused having no filter with having courage.
We have confused sarcasm with discernment.
We have confused public embarrassment with correction.
We have confused saying everything we think with spiritual maturity.
But self-control is fruit of the Spirit.
Read that again.
Self-control.
That includes what happens between the thought entering your mind and the words leaving your mouth.
Not every true thought deserves a microphone.
Not every observation deserves a comment.
Not every disagreement requires a response.
Not every failure needs to be announced.
Not every correction belongs in public.
Not every piece of truth belongs in every moment.
Sometimes holiness looks like opening your mouth.
Sometimes holiness looks like keeping it closed.
And perhaps nowhere is this more painful than inside families.
A child remembers being called stupid twenty years after the parent forgot saying it.
A wife remembers the joke her husband made about her body while everyone laughed.
A husband remembers the comparison his wife made between him and another man during an argument.
A teenager remembers being told, “You’ll never amount to anything.”
A church member remembers being publicly corrected for something that could have been handled privately.
A struggling believer remembers finally admitting what they were fighting—and wishing afterward they had never trusted anyone enough to confess it.
The speaker moved on.
The hearer carried the sentence home.
That is the terrifying thing about words.
You can finish speaking before they finish bleeding.
James understood this.
He compares the tongue to something tiny capable of setting an enormous forest ablaze.
A small flame.
A huge destruction.
Anyone who has lived long enough has watched this happen.
One text message.
One comment.
One accusation.
One rumor.
One sentence spoken while angry.
One humiliating joke.
One “I’m just saying what everybody else is thinking.”
And suddenly a relationship that took fifteen years to build is burning.
We often think the solution is simply to become nicer.
It is deeper than that.
Jesus teaches that words reveal the heart.
Our mouths are not independent machines malfunctioning above our shoulders.
Eventually the mouth exposes what has been living underneath it.
Pride speaks.
Jealousy speaks.
Bitterness speaks.
Fear speaks.
Unforgiveness speaks.
Insecurity speaks.
Self-righteousness speaks.
The tongue eventually gives the heart away.
So if you repeatedly destroy people with your words, the Gospel calls you to something deeper than learning better communication techniques.
It calls you to repentance.
Not shame without hope.
Repentance.
The beautiful, devastating mercy of God that allows us to stop defending what Christ wants to transform.
Maybe you have said things you wish you could pull back into your mouth.
Maybe you watched someone’s expression change the moment the words landed.
Maybe years have passed and you still remember what you said.
Maybe your child remembers too.
Maybe your spouse does.
Maybe your mother does.
Maybe the friend you lost does.
And perhaps you have spent years protecting yourself with one sentence:
“But it was true.”
Today, Jesus may be asking you to surrender that defense.
Because repentance does not begin when we explain ourselves better.
It begins when we stop explaining away what God is exposing.
You may need to say:
“I was wrong.”
Not...
“I’m sorry you were offended.”
Not...
“I’m sorry, but you know what I said was true.”
Not...
“I apologize if you misunderstood me.”
Just:
“I was wrong. What I said was cruel. I should not have spoken to you that way. Please forgive me.”
There is enormous spiritual power in an apology without an escape hatch.
And if you are reading this from the other side—if you were the person cut by somebody else’s words—hear this carefully:
What someone said about you is not automatically what God says about you.
People speak from anger.
People speak from wounds.
People speak from jealousy.
People speak from immaturity.
People speak from distorted perceptions.
Sometimes people even take a real weakness and turn it into your entire identity.
“You failed” becomes “You are a failure.”
“You made a foolish decision” becomes “You are stupid.”
“You sinned” becomes “You are worthless.”
“You disappointed me” becomes “Nobody could ever love you.”
That is not how the Gospel speaks.
The Gospel tells the truth about sin more seriously than our culture ever will.
We have sinned.
We cannot save ourselves.
We need forgiveness.
We need a Savior.
But then comes the scandal of grace.
Christ came for sinners.
Christ bore sin at the cross.
Christ rose from the dead.
Christ calls sinners to repent and believe.
And those who belong to Him are not sentenced to remain forever imprisoned inside the worst thing they have ever done.
That is why Gospel speech should sound different.
We can confront sin without erasing the sinner's humanity.
We can correct without humiliating.
We can disagree without dehumanizing.
We can warn without enjoying the fear in somebody’s eyes.
We can tell hard truths while tears are in our own eyes because we genuinely want the other person restored.
That is completely different from cruelty.
Ask yourself one question before your next difficult conversation:
Do I want this person healed—or do I want this person hurt?
Do not answer quickly.
Sit with it.
Because sometimes we call it correction when what we really want is retaliation.
Sometimes we say, “Someone needs to tell them,” when what we secretly mean is, “I want to be the one who finally puts them in their place.”
Sometimes we disguise bitterness as discernment.
Sometimes we disguise gossip as concern.
Sometimes we disguise humiliation as accountability.
Sometimes we disguise cruelty as honesty.
Jesus sees through every disguise.
And yet...
He still offers grace.
That may be the most beautiful part of this entire conversation.
The same Jesus who exposes the sin of our speech is willing to forgive the sinner speaking.
Peter once used his mouth to deny that he even knew Jesus.
Three times.
Imagine carrying those sentences after the crucifixion.
Imagine remembering your own voice.
“I do not know the man.”
But Peter's worst words did not become the final chapter of his story.
The risen Christ restored him.
Then the mouth that once denied Jesus became a mouth proclaiming Him.
That is Gospel transformation.
Jesus does not merely forgive what your tongue has done.
He can transform what your tongue becomes.
The mouth that once gossiped can begin protecting reputations.
The mouth that once cursed can begin blessing.
The mouth that once humiliated can begin encouraging.
The mouth that once lied can begin speaking truth.
The mouth that once tore a spouse down can begin building them up.
The parent who spoke death can begin speaking life.
The believer known for cruelty can become known for wisdom.
The tongue that once pierced like a sword can become, by God's transforming grace, an instrument of healing.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And maybe that rewriting begins today with one sentence you refuse to say.
One apology you finally make.
One conversation you choose to have privately instead of publicly.
One piece of gossip you refuse to repeat.
One comment you delete before posting.
One person you stop humiliating.
One moment when the Holy Spirit whispers, “Don't say it,” and for once...
you listen.
If this exposed something in you, do not hide behind embarrassment. Bring it into the light before Christ.
You do not have to explain the wound publicly.
But you also do not have to pretend words never hurt.
Read it yourself first. Pray over your own heart first. Then, if you believe it may genuinely help them, send it with humility.
Supporting Gospel-centered ministry can itself be one practical expression of generosity and partnership when it is done freely, prayerfully, and for God's glory.
Jesus wants more than your support.
He wants your heart.
He wants the bitterness you have justified.
The anger you have rehearsed.
The wounds you have weaponized.
The words you wish you could retrieve.
The shame you have carried because of what someone said about you.
Bring all of it to Him.
Repent where you have wounded.
Forgive as Christ gives you grace to forgive.
Seek reconciliation where it is wise and possible.
And surrender your tongue to the One who surrendered His life for you.
Because one day you may forget the argument.
You may forget what started it.
You may forget what room you were standing in.
But someone may remember your sentence for the rest of their life.
So before you say, “I’m just being honest”...
remember the sword.
Remember the healing.
And remember Jesus.
The tongue surrendered to Christ does not have to stop telling the truth—it learns to stop using truth as a knife.
